iterations.explanation: No user feedback. Dimensions split orthogonally by data placement, consistency semantics, replica economics, and explicitly stated tail-latency tradeoffs.

clusters.name: Repository Data Source-of-Truth Placement
clusters.description: Where authoritative Git data is stored or logically centralized (filesystem, KV store, split blob/metadata). Distinct from replication/consistency mechanics.

values.label: Centralized filesystem-backed object storage
values.description: Use a single authoritative filesystem/object store rather than distributing the underlying filesystem.

values.label: Distributed KV store for Git objects (rejected)
values.description: Keep repository objects in a distributed key-value store, rejected as a design alternative.

values.label: Split blob store and relational metadata (rejected)
values.description: Store blobs separately from metadata in different systems, rejected as an alternative architecture.

clusters.name: Consistency and Replication Semantics
clusters.description: How the system ensures correctness across replicas (strong, timely consistency vs other semantics), independent of replica-count economics.

relations.rationale: Stronger consistency typically increases write latency at scale and motivates careful replica-count control.

values.label: Strong, timely consistency required
values.description: Repository hosting must not tolerate eventual consistency; clients demand strong, timely consistency.

values.label: Consensus-based strong replication (Spokes)
values.description: Spokes uses strong consensus replication to meet consistency requirements.

clusters.name: Replica Count and Scale-Cost Tradeoffs
clusters.description: How many replicas are maintained (minimum vs more) under cost constraints, trading correctness/availability against resource usage.

relations.rationale: When using strong replication/consensus, limiting replicas can reduce availability/correctness margins.

values.label: Safe minimum replicas to reduce cost
values.description: Maintain a safe minimum replica count due to high cost from millions of tiny repos; trades correctness/availability.

clusters.name: Maintenance of Replication Performance Tail Latency
clusters.description: Which performance dimension is explicitly traded against correctness/consistency (e.g., tail write latency), orthogonal to replica count.

relations.rationale: The documented tradeoff is specifically between stronger consistency guarantees and higher tail-at-scale write latency.

values.label: Accept tail-at-scale write latency for consistency
values.description: Trading consistency guarantees for higher tail write latency as the dominant operational cost.

iterations.explanation: Added orthogonal axes: (5) write-path ordering (consensus-first vs log-first), (6) maintenance placement (primary-only compaction), (7) client/server responsibility partitioning (GVFS/Scalar). Kept existing consistency/replica/latency dimensions; extended consistency with WAL-derived truth. Added (8) as a lightweight framing axis for server-scale distribution constraints to capture scaling-vs-distribution constraint narratives not covered by other dimensions. Modifications reflect new docs about WAL, S3-based WAL, primary-only compaction tradeoffs, and client virtualization while preserving prior consensus/replica/latency structure.

clusters.name: Write Path Source of Truth and Ordering
clusters.description: Whether client-visible correctness relies on pre-consensus application or on logging then deriving state; distinguishes consensus-first from WAL-first systems.

relations.rationale: WAL-first designs correspond to non-consensus-first semantics (log recorded before acting), weakening the need for immediate consensus-driven state application.
WAL-first designs typically pair with object/log backends for the durable record of operations, though not strictly required.

values.label: Consensus-first: agree before acting
values.description: Changes are applied based on agreeing via consensus/replication before they take effect as authoritative state.

values.label: Log-first: write-ahead logging records before truth
values.description: Operations are first recorded in a write-ahead log, and authoritative repository truth is derived after.

clusters.name: Replicated Storage Maintenance Responsibility Placement
clusters.description: Where maintenance/compaction work runs in a replicated system (e.g., primary-only vs distributed), trading CPU and bandwidth usage across nodes.

relations.rationale: Compaction-placement strategies are most relevant when multiple replicas exist and synchronize derived/compacted results.
Both consensus-based and WAL-derived architectures may require background maintenance, but maintenance placement is a separate operational axis.

values.label: Primary-only compaction
values.description: Compaction/maintenance is performed only on the primary, reducing replica CPU but shifting load to primary.

clusters.name: Client vs Server Responsibility Partitioning
clusters.description: How responsibilities for caching/transfer/consistency handling are divided between clients and the server, independently of storage or replication semantics.

relations.rationale: Shifting consistency handling to clients reduces server-side complexity and changes where correctness work is performed, but does not fully determine consensus vs WAL semantics.
Client virtualization often accompanies server simplification, but source-of-truth placement can still vary independently.

values.label: Client-side virtualization (GVFS/Scalar)
values.description: Scale by shifting caching/transfer/consistency handling to clients while keeping the Git server simpler.

clusters.name: Distribution Scaling Mechanism and Constraints
clusters.description: What mechanism frames scaling difficulty or the dominant lever for server-scale distribution (replication/consistency constraints vs broader distribution constraints).

relations.rationale: Server-scale distribution constraints are repeatedly tied to replication/consistency decisions, especially in Spokes/WAL transitions.
The scaling story often aligns with whether the system is consensus-first or log-first.

values.label: Replication/consistency constrained distribution at server scale
values.description: Server-scale repository distribution is framed as difficult because replication and consistency requirements constrain how distribution can work.

saturation_history.rationale: All open codes are covered by existing taxonomy dimensions: (1) Consistency requirements and Spokes’ consensus-based strong replication map directly to Dimension 2 (values 2.1 and 2.2). (2) The explicit tradeoff between stronger consistency and higher tail-at-scale write latency maps to Dimension 4 (value 4.1). (3) The rejected storage-placement alternatives—distributing the filesystem, using a distributed KV store for Git objects, and splitting blob storage vs relational metadata—map to Dimension 1’s “source-of-truth placement” variants (values 1.1–1.3) as rejected alternatives. (4) Spokes’ “safe minimum replica count” and the replica-count/cost vs correctness/availability tradeoff map to Dimension 3 (value 3.1). Therefore there are no remaining relevant uncovered architectural concepts revealed by this minibatch.

All relevant open codes are subsumed by existing taxonomy dimensions: (1) server-scale distribution constrained by replication/consistency → covered by Dimension 8 (Distribution Scaling Mechanism and Constraints). (2) architectural tradeoff scaling distribution while preserving correctness across replicas → covered by Dimensions 2/4/8. (3–4) shift from pre-consensus replication to WAL-first plus deriving truth after logs → covered by Dimensions 2 (log-first operations), 5 (Log-first: write-ahead logging records before truth), and 8. (5–7) primary-only compaction and related tradeoffs (CPU/bandwidth) → covered by Dimension 6 (Replicated Storage Maintenance Responsibility Placement). (8,12,15) migration away from Spokes and consensus-replicated hosting → covered by Dimension 2 (Consensus-based strong replication) and 8. (9,10) S3-backed write-ahead logs and WAL as primary scaling mechanism → the taxonomic axis is the log-first model (Dimensions 2 and 5); specific “S3-backed” storage backend is not a distinct axis beyond source-of-durable-log mechanism already captured by the WAL/log-first dimensions. (11) Cursor-specific transition to Continuity/Origin → covered in substance by the WAL-first/log-derived architecture dimensions (2/5/8), even if the taxonomy doesn’t name the product. (13–14) “durable pets” / correctness-prioritized over elastic scaling assumptions → captured as the same correctness-vs-elasticity intent expressed by strong consistency requirements (Dimension 2) and by the correctness-first tradeoff context (Dimensions 2/4/8). (16–17) shift from early GitHub experiments to Spokes → covered by Dimension 2/8 framing (consensus vs other approaches). (18–19) real Git repositories replicated via consensus → covered by Dimension 2 (Consensus-based strong replication). (20) adding replication/enforcing consistency as scaling levers → covered by Dimension 2 and 3 (replica economics) plus 8. (21–22) GVFS/Scalar client-side virtualization and shifting caching/transfer/consistency responsibilities to clients → covered by Dimension 7 (Client vs Server Responsibility Partitioning).
